title: Urban Heat Islands
subject: environmental science
transcript: Okay, let's pick up where we left off last week. We talked about how cities change the landscape, and today I want to look at one consequence: the urban heat island effect. Basically, cities tend to be warmer than the countryside around them, sometimes by as much as five degrees Celsius at night. Why? A big part of it is surfaces. Asphalt and concrete absorb sunlight during the day and release that heat slowly after dark. In a forest or a field, plants cool the air by releasing water through their leaves, but a parking lot can't do that. Here's an example that surprised a lot of people. When researchers measured temperatures across one large city on a summer afternoon, a neighborhood with lots of trees was nearly four degrees cooler than a neighborhood just two kilometers away with almost none. Same weather, same sunshine. The only real difference was the tree cover. So this isn't just about comfort. Higher temperatures mean more air conditioning, which means more energy use, and during heat waves, more health emergencies. Now, cities have started fighting back, and next I want to walk you through a few of the strategies they're using, starting with something called cool roofs.
